title: In vivo imaging of a PVD neuron in Caenorhabditis elegans
protocol: Dissolve 2% (w/v) agarose in M9 buffer using a microwave oven until fully dissolved.
Maintain the solution at 65°C on a hot plate or metal bath during preparation.
Optionally, aliquot 5 mL of the agarose solution into a 15 mL Corning centrifuge tube and store at 4°C for up to 2 months.
When needed, heat an aliquoted tube in an 80°C metal bath until completely dissolved.
Place three clear microscope slides in parallel.
Paste adhesive tapes on the two side slides to create approximately 200 μm thick space compared to the middle slide.
Add one drop of 2% molten agarose onto the center of the middle slide.
Lay down another slide orthogonally on the agarose drop.
Separate the slides with the agarose pad so that the pad remains attached to one slide.
Store the slide in a humidity chamber at room temperature.
Add 5 μL of 5 mM levamisole onto an agarose pad.
Pick 10–20 worms at late L4 stage into the levamisole solution on the pad and gently swing the pick to spread the worms sparsely.
Allow the worms to be anesthetized for 1–2 min in 5 mM Levamisole.
Do not exceed adding more than 5 μL of levamisole solution to the agarose pad for worm immobilization.
Place the coverslip as fast as possible if limiting volume to avoid worms from dehydrating.
Use late L4 stage worms for imaging PVD neurons when dendrites are fully developed and branches are not exuberant.
Reduce residual OP50 E. coli on the pad to minimize background fluorescence and worm movement during imaging.
Spread mounted worms sparsely on the slide to allow for clear identification of individual worms under microscopy.
Pick worms gently to avoid stressing PVD neurons, which are vulnerable to stress-induced degeneration.
Cover the worms with a coverslip.
Store the slide in a humidity chamber for 5-10 minutes before imaging.
Anesthetize the worms for 1–2 minutes.
Cover the anesthetized worms immediately after anesthesia.
Position the slide on the microscope stage and focus under low magnification using bright field illumination to find separated worms with a perfect lateral view of PVD neuron.
Ensure that the worms remain still throughout the imaging period.
Avoid bubbles when covering the sample with a coverslip to prevent interference with fluorescence projection.
Switch to 20× magnification.
Turn on the 488 nm laser.
Select worms with whole branches (1°, 2°, 3°, and 4°) of a PVD neuron for imaging.
Switch to high magnification (40×/1.3 N.A oil immersion objective).
Focus on the PVD neuron.
Choose a field without worms sticking to each other.
Acquire microscopy images.
Adjust major parameters (Channel, laser intensity, exposure times, pinhole and bit depth) appropriately.
Ensure clear visualization of the PVD soma and all its branches (1°, 2°, 3°, and 4°).
Enhance excitation intensity to clearly show the 4° branches.
Image 15–30 Z steps at a rate of 0.5 μm per step until all branches can be photographed clearly.
Use 3–4 visual fields under 40× magnification to image the whole PVD neuron.
Open ∗.nd format images with ImageJ software (Schneider et al., 2012).
Convert the image type to 8 bit and change color settings to grayscale.
Generate a maximum-intensity Z projection from the images.
Adjust brightness/contrast for optimal fluorescent intensity and minimal background signal.
Capture screen and calculate scale bar.
Assemble images from 3–4 visual fields to obtain a complete dendrite structure of a single PVD neuron.
